newsitem.title: MEXICO: Cuban diver fails to break free-diving record.
newsitem.headline: Cuban diver fails to break free-diving record.

text.p: A Cuban diver on Sunday failed in his bid to break a world record by diving 443 feet (135 metres) underwater while holding his breath, and alarmed spectators by staying down nearly twice as long as expected.

In a dangerous effort broadcast live on Mexican television, commentators became audibly agitated when Cuban exile Pipin Ferreras remained underwater for more than four minutes. He was meant to emerge in two minutes and 30 seconds.
"We're worried, because now we're out of time completely," a Televisa reporter said as the clock ticked, and cameras were trained on the Pacific Ocean waiting for Ferreras' reappearance.
When he finally emerged after four minutes 35 seconds, there was a cry of "Here comes Pipin," and relieved cheers.
Ferreras, a Cuban exile who started diving as a spear fisherman in Havana, blamed his failure on some of the flotilla of 50 boats that gathered in this tourist resort to watch his attempt.
He said the boats, some of which were attached to his diving platform, drifted on the wind, dragging the platform.

A cable descending from the platform was supposed to guide Ferreras into a 985-foot (300-metre) underwater canyon. But it also drifted, and the bid was aborted by fellow divers when Ferreras was about to slam into the canyon wall at a depth of 395 feet (120 metres).

"My assistant divers down there stopped me, they gave me a (breathing) regulator and that's how I got back up to the surface," Ferreras told Televisa, adding he would repeat the attempt on Monday or Tuesday.
"I can't leave this place without the record. The only thing is the next time I'm not going to do it publically," he said, disappointment etched on his face.

Supporters of the bald 34-year-old diver were confident he would, on a second attempt, steal the record of 430 feet (131 metres) held by Humberto Pellizare of Italy, who eclipsed Ferreras' record in June.
As a youth, Ferreras had stumbled on to the sport by accident while trying to make a living along Havana's famous boardwalk, diving for fish with a speargun.

At first, he made friendly bets with tourists that he could swim to unthinkable depths without the benefit of scuba gear. Now, he makes a living from corporate sponsorship. The logo of Mexico's main phone company, Telmex, was splashed across his wet suit.
